network.overall_strategy: Construct a connected, target-focused hypothesis network containing ten distinct reaction sequences, not ten experimentally established syntheses. P1-P8 are explicitly related combinations of three chemically motivated choices: guanidination before or after C3 nitrile reduction, sulfide versus a proposed sulfite photoreductant at that reduction, and direct versus proposed thioamide-mediated hydration of the final aminonitrile. P9-P10 examine free-monomer and post-oligomerization guanidination of discharge-derived ornithine. The strongest scaffold is the experimentally supported arginine aminonitrile chemistry of Patel et al. (2015); its conversion to quantified free arginine remains an end-to-end experimental gap. Sulfite substitutions, terminal thioamide processing, and cyanamide-based peptide conversion are explicitly conditional hypotheses. No unidentified glutamate-to-ornithine bridge or contested direct Fischer-Tropsch arginine edge is presented as an established reaction. All starting materials are simple molecular feedstocks, but their simultaneous availability is not assumed: cyanide concentration, cyanamide supply, sulfide availability, copper speciation, and staged mixing remain geochemical requirements. Conditions are proposed environmental windows, not claims that every listed window was experimentally validated. Neutral molecular formulas represent acid-base families; no enantioselectivity is assumed. Sulfur and sulfate are formal terminal redox bookkeeping products, not claims of exclusive measured sulfur speciation. The schema lacks a byproduct role, so connected byproducts and competing sinks use the intermediate role. This is a target-focused network, not an exhaustive inventory of mixture products.

reactions.name: Copper-mediated hydrocyanation of acetylene

conditions.other: Anoxic acetylene-bearing water; cyanide and copper availability required; perform before introducing sulfide that could precipitate copper.

reactions.mechanism: Copper-assisted addition of hydrogen cyanide across acetylene produces acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This supplies the C3 entry substrate used in the arginine branch of Patel et al. (2015). Cu(I) is chemically justified for this coupling rather than added as a generic mineral catalyst. Cyanide storage and subsequent concentration have environmental support from Toner and Catling (2019), but acetylene delivery, copper speciation, and useful natural reaction rates remain requirements.

reactions.name: Ammonia conjugate addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich solution; approximately pH 8-10; control residence time and substrate concentration.

reactions.mechanism: Aza-Michael addition places an amino group at the terminal carbon of acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) use beta-aminopropionitrile as the shared entry intermediate for the arginine/proline chemistry. No mineral catalyst is intrinsically needed. Further cyanoethylation and other acrylonitrile reactions can reduce selectivity, so this is not assumed to be quantitative.

reactions.name: Sulfide-driven photoreduction of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic UV irradiation; laboratory precedent near 254 nm; mildly neutral-to-alkaline water; rapid downstream cyanamide trapping.

reactions.mechanism: Photogenerated reducing equivalents reduce the nitrile to an imine-level intermediate, whose hydrolysis gives the aldehyde and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: The transformation is part of Patel et al. (2015). Sulfide is a reagent, not merely a mineral agent. Ranjan et al. (2018) identify sulfide abundance as a limitation, and dissolved Fe2+ and copper can further sequester it. Elemental sulfur represents a balanced terminal oxidation sink; actual sulfur photoproducts need not be exclusively S8.

reactions.name: Proposed sulfite-driven photoreduction of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic UV-exposed sulfite-bearing solution; approximately pH 7.5-9; no molecular oxygen; substrate-specific performance unmeasured.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed sulfite photoionization supplies reducing equivalents for nitrile reduction and hydrolysis; sulfate is the formal fully oxidized sulfur endpoint.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this substrate. Ranjan et al. (2018) motivate more available SO2-derived sulfur species as alternatives where sulfur only supplies electrons, while Patel et al. (2015) establish the sulfide-based substrate transformation. Neither source establishes this particular substitution, its selectivity, or exclusive sulfate formation. It tests a real sulfur-supply constraint rather than assuming sulfite can replace sulfur-incorporation steps.

reactions.name: Aldehyde-stage cyanamide trapping and guanidine-ring formation

conditions.other: Cyanamide available during or immediately after aldehyde generation; proposed pH 7-9; avoid prolonged storage of the untrapped aminoaldehyde.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanamide capture at the aldehyde, followed by intramolecular addition involving the pendant amine, generates a cyclic guanidinated hemiaminal.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) identify efficient aldehyde-stage capture as more effective than direct aminonitrile guanidination. The six-membered hemiaminal is the structural representation used here; its environmental microstate distribution is not supplied by the research summary. Cyanamide hydrolysis and other competing reactions prevent treating its concentration as fixed.

reactions.name: Early guanidination of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.other: Concentrated cyanamide and aminonitrile; mildly alkaline conditions; unreacted feedstocks expected.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal amino group attacks cyanamide's electrophilic carbon, followed by proton transfers to the substituted guanidine.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) explicitly describe this guanidination as relatively inefficient. It is retained as a genuine chemical alternative, not assigned equal performance to aldehyde-stage capture. Cyanamide persistence and competing reactivity are consistent with Steinman et al. (1964), but useful environmental conversion is not established.

reactions.name: Sulfide photoreduction of the early-guanidinated nitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic UV irradiation; staged sulfide addition; copper must remain photochemically available.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile photoreduction and imine hydrolysis generate a guanidinated aldehyde that cyclizes to its hemiaminal reservoir.
reactions.reasoning: This encodes the early-guanidination branch described in the reaction logic of Patel et al. (2015). Its environmental yield is not independently established, especially because the preceding guanidination is inefficient. Ranjan et al. (2018) provide the same sulfur-availability caution as for the unguanidinated reduction.

reactions.name: Proposed sulfite photoreduction of the early-guanidinated nitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic UV irradiation of sulfite-bearing water; approximately pH 7.5-9; guanidino-group survival must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed sulfite-derived reducing equivalents reduce the nitrile, followed by hydrolysis and intramolecular hemiaminal formation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific extension of the sulfur-source argument in Ranjan et al. (2018), using the sulfide-route scaffold of Patel et al. (2015). Guanidinium effects on electron capture, competing reduction, and product partitioning are unresolved. This edge does not claim experimentally demonstrated arginine chemistry with sulfite.

reactions.name: Ring opening of the guanidinated hemiaminal

conditions.other: Reversible ring-chain equilibrium; subsequent cyanide capture can consume the open-chain fraction.

reactions.mechanism: Hemiaminal C-N bond cleavage restores the aldehyde without changing molecular composition.
reactions.reasoning: This is a mechanistic resolution of aldehyde-equivalent reactivity in Patel et al. (2015), not a claim of an independently isolated open-chain aldehyde or a measured equilibrium constant. Separating the isomers makes the carbonyl chemistry explicit without treating a cyclic hemiaminal as a permanently free aldehyde.

reactions.name: First cyanide homologation of the guanidinated aldehyde

conditions.other: Cyanide introduced after aldehyde formation; approximately pH 7-9; reversible cyanohydrin formation.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition to the aldehyde carbonyl produces an alpha-hydroxynitrile and adds one carbon to the future amino-acid backbone.
reactions.reasoning: This homologation belongs to the explicit arginine-precursor sequence of Patel et al. (2015). It requires an accessible aldehyde fraction and adequate cyanide activity; mineral-mediated cyanide concentration is environmentally plausible but not demonstrated as an integrated operation with this branch (Toner and Catling, 2019).

reactions.name: Sulfide addition to the first cyanohydrin nitrile

conditions.other: HS-/H2S available; mildly alkaline water; limit sulfide loss to volatilization and FeS precipitation.

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic sulfide addition to the nitrile and proton transfers form an alpha-hydroxythioamide.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) use thioamide chemistry in this homologation sequence. Here sulfur is incorporated into the substrate, so sulfite cannot simply replace sulfide as an electron donor. The sulfide-concentration limitations emphasized by Ranjan et al. (2018) therefore remain even in pathways using an earlier sulfite photoreduction.

reactions.name: Photochemical deoxygenation of the alpha-hydroxythioamide

conditions.other: Anoxic UV exposure with sulfide-derived reducing equivalents; irradiation and reagent additions staged.

reactions.mechanism: Net reductive replacement of the alpha-hydroxyl group by hydrogen produces the deoxygenated thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: This is a key backbone-building transformation in Patel et al. (2015), not ordinary thermal dehydration. UV availability is physically plausible at suitable early-Earth surfaces (Ranjan and Sasselov, 2017), but sulfur loading can also suppress the radiation required for the reaction (Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Photoreductive conversion of the thioamide to a homologated aldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic sulfide-assisted UV chemistry; water participates in hydrolytic workup of reduced intermediates.

reactions.mechanism: Net thioamide photoreduction and hydrolytic processing generate the aldehyde, ammonia, and sulfur products.
reactions.reasoning: The thioamide-to-aldehyde continuation is part of Patel et al. (2015). This node is a net transformation rather than an elementary mechanism. H2S appears on both sides because photodonor oxidation and release of substrate-bound sulfur can offset in the net balance; its experimental presence is still required. S8 is a formal sulfur sink, not a uniquely characterized coproduct.

reactions.name: Second cyanide homologation to the terminal cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Fresh cyanide addition after the preceding photoreduction; approximately pH 7-9.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde, installing the carbon that will become arginine's carboxyl carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support this second homologation in the arginine branch. The product has six total carbons: five in the eventual amino-acid backbone and one in the guanidino group. Reagent sequencing is necessary; simultaneous exposure of all feedstocks to every earlier step is not assumed.

reactions.name: Strecker-type conversion of the terminal cyanohydrin to arginine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich stage after photochemical homologation; approximately pH 8-10; avoid unnecessary further irradiation.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanohydrin dissociation permits aldehyde-imine equilibration; cyanide capture of the imine produces the alpha-aminonitrile. This is not direct displacement of hydroxide.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) identify compound 46 as the arginine alpha-aminonitrile precursor. This is the strongest experimentally supported arginine-specific endpoint in the supplied de novo sequence. It must not be represented as an isolated, quantitatively established yield of free arginine.

reactions.name: Hydration of arginine aminonitrile to argininamide

conditions.other: Candidate acidic pool or later acidic episode; approximately pH 1-3; extended residence may be necessary; protect from continued strong UV.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-assisted water addition to the nitrile followed by tautomerization produces the carboxamide.
reactions.reasoning: Chemically expected Strecker-product processing, but speculative as an environmentally validated step for this exact substrate. Patel et al. (2015) establish the aminonitrile rather than an end-to-end free-arginine yield. Hydration rate, aminonitrile decomposition, and guanidino-group survival must be measured under the proposed conditions.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of argininamide to free arginine

conditions.other: Candidate pH 1-2; prolonged hydrolysis followed by cooling; product represented without its protonation-state counterions.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the activated amide carbonyl; C-N cleavage releases ammonia/ammonium and forms the carboxylic acid.
reactions.reasoning: This is the chemically expected final hydrolysis, but its useful rate and selectivity within the stated prebiotic window are not established by Patel et al. (2015). It is a bottleneck, not an assumed quantitative workup. Harsh laboratory hydrolysis cannot be silently substituted for environmental validation.

reactions.name: Proposed sulfide capture of arginine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Candidate HS--bearing water at approximately pH 8-10; subsequent sulfur removal must occur in a separate chemical stage.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed sulfide addition to the terminal nitrile gives the corresponding alpha-aminothioamide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate extension, not a demonstrated arginine reaction in the supplied research. Patel et al. (2015) support nitrile-to-thioamide chemistry earlier in the same scaffold, which motivates testing an alternative endpoint in sulfide-bearing water. The alpha-amino and guanidino substituents may change reactivity; no rate enhancement or yield advantage is asserted.

reactions.name: Proposed hydrolytic sulfur replacement in arginine thioamide

conditions.other: Candidate pH 1-3; anoxic H2S removal by gas exchange could favor sulfur release; reaction rate is unknown.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed hydrolytic replacement of thiocarbonyl sulfur by oxygen produces argininamide and hydrogen sulfide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and potentially rate-limiting. No supplied study establishes this conversion for arginine thioamide at these temperatures. Patel et al. (2015) motivate examining sulfur-containing nitrile-processing chemistry, but do not validate this endpoint. Competing cleavage pathways or excessive thioamide persistence could invalidate P5-P8.

reactions.name: Coarse-grained volcanic-discharge production of ornithine

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk collector; discharge is a nonequilibrium energy source
conditions.other: Anoxic reducing gas/steam mixture exposed to electrical discharge, followed by aqueous collection and any necessary precursor hydrolysis; local discharge temperatures are not the bulk temperature.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved radical, carbonyl, nitrile, and nitrogen-incorporation chemistry produces a broad collected mixture containing ornithine or hydrolysable ornithine precursors.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied report attributes ornithine evidence to the volcanic-discharge archive analyzed by Johnson et al. (2008) and subsequent work in that lineage. This is an explicitly coarse-grained product-generation edge, not an identified elementary synthesis or selective preparation. Hydrogen closes a formal target-specific atom balance; it is not an experimentally assigned ornithine-specific coproduct. Ornithine yield, hydrolysis dependence, and accumulation remain uncertainties.

reactions.name: Candidate free-ornithine guanidination with cyanamide

conditions.other: Concentrated ornithine and cyanamide; candidate mildly alkaline conditions; side-chain versus alpha-amino guanidination must be quantified.

reactions.mechanism: The ornithine delta-amino group attacks cyanamide, installing the guanidino carbon and two additional nitrogen atoms.
reactions.reasoning: Longo et al. (2020) establish the chemical concept of ornithine-to-arginine conversion and identify cyanamide as a simple possible guanidinating reagent. Their quantitative peptide experiments do not establish this free-monomer cyanamide reaction in a naturalistic pool. Accordingly, environmental rate, regioselectivity, yield, and compatibility with discharge mixtures remain speculative.

reactions.name: Candidate alpha-linked ornithine dimer formation

conditions.other: Concentrated dry-down phase of wet-dry cycling; no enzyme or modern coupling reagent; alpha-linkage selectivity is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Intermolecular condensation of an ornithine carboxyl group with another ornithine alpha-amino group gives an alpha-linked dipeptide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative productive edge included to represent the smallest explicit post-polymerization route, not as an efficient dimer synthesis. Frenkel-Pinter et al. (2019) show that ornithine undergoes competing lactamization and problematic oligomerization. Branched products and low conversion are expected risks; rxn_027 records the key lactam sink.

reactions.name: Candidate cyanamide guanidination of ornithine dipeptide side chains

conditions.other: Rehydrated peptide-containing solution; candidate pH 8-10; sufficient cyanamide for both side chains; N-terminal modification is a competing reaction.

reactions.mechanism: Guanidination of both ornithine delta-amino groups converts the model dipeptide to arginylarginine without requiring peptide-bond cleavage.
reactions.reasoning: Longo et al. (2020) demonstrate aqueous postsynthetic ornithine-to-arginine conversion on model polypeptides, but not this exact dipeptide with cyanamide under primitive conditions. The reagent substitution and substrate-specific conversion are speculative. Complete conversion from the laboratory study is not transferred to this candidate environmental reaction.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic release of arginine from arginylarginine

conditions.other: Candidate acidic rehydration episode; prolonged residence; free-arginine recovery must exceed guanidino-group and backbone degradation.

reactions.mechanism: Peptide-bond hydrolysis releases two arginine molecules; the coefficient is implicit rather than represented by repeated IDs.
reactions.reasoning: Ordinary peptide hydrolysis makes monomer release chemically possible, but this environmental closure is speculative. Longo et al. (2020) support peptide-bound arginine formation, not a complete prebiotic synthesis and hydrolysis sequence yielding free arginine. This route is relevant to peptide recycling, not necessarily efficient monomer production.

reactions.name: Competing cyanamide hydrolysis

conditions.other: Background aqueous loss; rate depends strongly on temperature, pH, and other solutes.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition to cyanamide's nitrile functionality yields urea.
reactions.reasoning: Included as a chemically justified cyanamide sink so that guanidination does not receive an unlimited reagent budget. Steinman et al. (1964) support cyanamide's aqueous persistence and reactivity, not a quantified loss rate in this network. Its environmental kinetic importance is therefore an unmeasured modeling assumption.

reactions.name: Competing cyanamide dimerization

conditions.other: Concentrated cyanamide, especially during evaporative concentration; pH-dependent conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Addition of one cyanamide molecule to another forms dicyandiamide.
reactions.reasoning: This known chemical possibility is a speculative environmental sink in the present network: the supplied research does not quantify it in an arginine-producing mixture. It addresses the cyanamide-budget gap identified in the report rather than asserting support from the condensation experiments of Steinman et al. (1964) for a particular dimerization rate.

reactions.name: Competing ornithine delta-lactam formation

conditions.other: Dry-down or low-water-activity phase; intramolecular condensation competes with intermolecular peptide formation.

reactions.mechanism: The delta-amino group attacks the carboxyl group, producing a six-membered lactam with loss of water.
reactions.reasoning: Frenkel-Pinter et al. (2019) experimentally identify ornithine lactamization as a competing process in prebiotic oligomerization. The environmental rate within this proposed temperature window remains unquantified. This sink prevents presenting the ornithine-first peptide pathway as an automatically productive detour.

pathways.name: Aldehyde-stage guanidination with sulfide photochemistry and direct hydration
pathways.description: Best-supported precursor scaffold: cyanamide traps the C3 aminoaldehyde, followed by two homologation stages and aminonitrile formation. Free arginine remains conditional on successful nitrile and amide hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Early nitrile guanidination with sulfide photochemistry and direct hydration
pathways.description: Guanidination occurs before C3 nitrile reduction. This is a real but inefficient entry alternative that converges with P1 at the guanidinated hemiaminal; the same unvalidated environmental hydrolysis endpoint remains.

pathways.name: Sulfite-assisted aminoaldehyde entry with direct terminal hydration
pathways.description: Conditional P1 variant replacing only the first nitrile photoreduction with a proposed sulfite-driven reaction. Sulfide remains necessary for downstream sulfur incorporation and established photochemical transformations.

pathways.name: Early guanidination and proposed sulfite reduction with direct hydration
pathways.description: Combines experimentally inefficient early guanidination with an unvalidated sulfite reduction of the guanidinated nitrile. It is a hypothesis sequence, not evidence for an independently demonstrated sulfite arginine synthesis.

pathways.name: Aldehyde-stage guanidination with proposed terminal thioamide processing
pathways.description: Uses the P1 precursor scaffold but tests sulfide addition and hydrolytic sulfur replacement as an alternative route from aminonitrile to argininamide. Both terminal sulfur-processing reactions require substrate-specific validation.

pathways.name: Early guanidination with proposed terminal thioamide processing
pathways.description: Combines the early-guanidination entry with the hypothetical terminal aminothioamide route. Low entry conversion and uncertain sulfur removal make this less secure than the shared precursor chemistry alone.

pathways.name: Sulfite-assisted aminoaldehyde entry and terminal thioamide processing
pathways.description: A combinatorial candidate testing both a more available early photoreductant and an alternative aminonitrile-processing module. It is not a sulfide-free route and has multiple independently unvalidated edges.

pathways.name: Early guanidination, proposed sulfite reduction, and terminal thioamide processing
pathways.description: The most conditional shared-scaffold variant: inefficient early guanidination, substrate-unvalidated sulfite photoreduction, and hypothetical terminal thioamide processing precede free-arginine formation.

pathways.name: Volcanic-discharge ornithine followed by free-monomer guanidination
pathways.description: A mechanistically independent carbon-skeleton entry: collect ornithine from broad discharge chemistry and test cyanamide guanidination. Ornithine concentration, alpha-versus-delta selectivity, and naturalistic free-arginine yield remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Ornithine oligomerization, postsynthetic guanidination, and monomer release
pathways.description: An explicit minimal peptide-recycling hypothesis: discharge-derived ornithine forms an alpha-linked dimer, side chains are guanidinated, and peptide hydrolysis releases arginine. Ornithine lactamization, linkage selectivity, primitive guanidinating conditions, and hydrolysis rates are major bottlenecks.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest pathway. Its carbon-skeleton construction and aldehyde-stage guanidination closely follow the experimentally supported arginine-aminonitrile chemistry summarized for Patel et al. (2015). Conversion through argininamide to free arginine is chemically conventional, but substrate-specific yields, compatible hydrolysis conditions and end-to-end recovery are not established here. Surface labels and acknowledgments of geochemical requirements do not specify the operating conditions needed to assess environmental integration.
suggestions: Measure arginine-aminonitrile hydration and argininamide hydrolysis across explicit pH, temperature and residence-time windows, quantifying free arginine and competing products.
Map the guanidinated intermediates to explicit structures and Patel compound identifiers, with reaction-level citations distinguishing demonstrated steps from extrapolations.
Specify concentrations, irradiation conditions, copper speciation and staged additions, then test the complete sequence with quantitative product and recovery measurements.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Early guanidination is chemically plausible, but Patel et al. (2015) report relatively inefficient direct guanidination of beta-aminopropionitrile. Product formation in a mixture containing residual cyanamide does not by itself establish how much material follows rxn_007 rather than aldehyde-stage trapping. The downstream scaffold remains coherent, with the same unresolved free-arginine hydrolysis and environmental-integration requirements as P1.
suggestions: Quantify formation and photoreduction of mol_013 independently, using controls that distinguish early guanidination from subsequent cyanamide trapping.
Measure how cyanamide hydrolysis and dimerization affect productive guanidination under the selected conditions.
Demonstrate terminal hydrolysis and free-arginine recovery using the actual upstream reaction mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sulfite substitution is conservation-consistent and reasonably identified as a hypothesis. Ranjan et al. (2018) support favorable sulfite availability and motivate photochemical alternatives, but do not establish this substrate-specific reduction or its compatibility with cyanamide trapping. Retaining sulfide for downstream sulfur-incorporating chemistry is appropriate. Free-arginine formation still depends on unvalidated terminal hydrolysis conditions.
suggestions: Compare sulfite and sulfide reduction of beta-aminopropionitrile under matched irradiation, measuring aldehyde yield, donor consumption and side products.
Test whether sulfite/bisulfite carbonyl adduct formation competes with cyanamide interception of the aminoaldehyde.
Specify the photochemical operating window and demonstrate subsequent hydrolysis to analytically confirmed free arginine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway combines experimentally inefficient early guanidination with a substrate-specific sulfite photoreduction that remains unestablished in the supplied literature. General sulfite photoreductant plausibility does not demonstrate selective conversion of the guanidinated nitrile to mol_014. Connectivity and downstream carbon accounting are sound, but these entry reactions and the final hydrolysis prevent high confidence in completed synthesis.
suggestions: Test rxn_008 using independently characterized mol_013, with controls for guanidino-group retention and competing photochemistry.
Report pH-dependent substrate speciation, irradiation requirements and any necessary sensitizer or copper species.
Quantify material recovery through early guanidination, photoreduction and final hydrolysis rather than extrapolating from aldehyde-stage trapping.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route to arginine aminonitrile retains the strongest supported scaffold. However, the demonstrated homologation-stage thioamide chemistry does not establish sulfide capture and hydrolytic sulfur replacement for this terminal alpha-aminonitrile. Both proposed reactions are balanced and chemically conceivable, but their rates, selectivity and suitable conditions are missing. This alternative therefore does not yet resolve the free-arginine endpoint gap.
suggestions: Prepare and structurally characterize mol_023, then measure its formation from arginine aminonitrile under specified sulfide conditions.
Determine whether aqueous processing produces argininamide, arginine or competing products, without assuming water alone gives useful sulfur replacement.
Compare terminal thioamide processing directly with nitrile hydration using free-arginine recovery as the endpoint.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The intermediate sequence is coherent, but productive flux depends on inefficient early guanidination and unvalidated terminal thioamide processing. Patel et al. (2015) support the broader scaffold, not an established free-arginine endpoint through rxn_018 and rxn_019. Environmental feasibility remains conditional on specifying both the photochemical stages and the subsequent sulfur-replacement and amide-hydrolysis conditions.
suggestions: Establish yields for the early-guanidinated branch separately from residual-cyanamide aldehyde trapping.
Validate terminal thioamide formation and processing independently before integrating them with upstream photochemistry.
Measure cyanamide consumption, sulfur speciation and product recovery during the transitions between reaction stages.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a connected, balanced hypothesis with unresolved chemistry at sulfite-driven entry and terminal thioamide processing. Sulfite availability does not validate rxn_004, while earlier thioamide homologation does not validate rxn_018 or rxn_019. The network correctly retains downstream sulfide requirements, so sulfite substitution should not be interpreted as eliminating the need for a local sulfide source.
suggestions: Validate sulfite reduction and terminal thioamide processing as separate modules using structurally verified substrates.
Quantify residual sulfite effects on cyanamide trapping and subsequent sulfide chemistry.
Provide a staged reagent-supply and recovery model, including the sulfide still required for homologation and terminal thioamide formation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The molecular sequence is internally consistent, but completion depends on inefficient early guanidination, unvalidated sulfite reduction of its product and unvalidated terminal thioamide processing. Explicitly labeling these transformations as hypotheses is appropriate literature alignment, but does not establish productive flux through them. The lower confidence reflects these chemical uncertainties, not pathway length or reuse of intermediates.
suggestions: Require substrate-specific product identification and yields for rxn_008, rxn_018 and rxn_019 before treating this combination as a supported synthesis.
Benchmark early guanidination against aldehyde-stage trapping under comparable conditions.
Demonstrate that conditions selected for the proposed reactions preserve intermediates and permit subsequent quantified free-arginine release.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Discharge-derived ornithine followed by guanidination is a plausible strategy. The supplied volcanic-discharge literature supports ornithine occurrence, but rxn_020 is necessarily a coarse-grained mixture-production equation rather than an established selective transformation. Longo et al. (2020) support ornithine-to-arginine conversion conceptually, not quantitative free-ornithine conversion with cyanamide under the unspecified conditions here. Selectivity between the alpha- and delta-amino groups is a key target-identification issue.
suggestions: Parameterize the discharge source with measured ornithine yields, collection conditions and any hydrolysis used during analytical workup.
Test free ornithine plus cyanamide over defined concentration, pH and temperature ranges, measuring cyanamide loss and competing guanidination products.
Distinguish arginine from positional guanidination isomers using structural analysis and authentic standards, not molecular mass alone.
Quantify rainout, concentration and recovery before downstream guanidination.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The principal bottleneck is selective formation of the alpha-linked ornithine dimer without specified activation or drying conditions. Frenkel-Pinter et al. (2019) support substantial competing ornithine lactamization, appropriately represented by rxn_027. Longo et al. (2020) support postsynthetic peptide guanidination as a concept, but not this cyanamide protocol or its selectivity. Peptide hydrolysis to free arginine is plausible; however, the Biochemical label alone specifies neither an abiotic setting nor suitable reaction conditions.
suggestions: Specify and test an abiotic condensation protocol, quantifying alpha-linked dimer against delta-lactam, side-chain-linked products and other oligomers.
Demonstrate cyanamide-mediated conversion of both ornithine side chains while measuring N-terminal and other competing modifications.
Define drying, rehydration, guanidination and hydrolysis conditions with measured intermediate survival and recovery.
Quantify free arginine after peptide hydrolysis rather than treating peptide-bound guanidino-group formation as target achievement.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network has sufficient molecule and reaction nodes, is connected, and uses molecule IDs consistently. Accepting the deterministic check as ground truth, all 27 reactions conserve atoms and charge with appropriate coefficients: there are no conservation violations. Factors of eight associated with S8 are ordinary formula bookkeeping, not implausibly large stoichiometries. The formal sulfur products nevertheless do not establish actual photochemical sulfur speciation or kinetics. Connected competing sinks rxn_025 and rxn_026 are chemically plausible, and rxn_027 reflects the literature-supported ornithine lactamization challenge; their rates relative to productive chemistry remain unspecified. Literature alignment is good in distinguishing the Patel et al. aminonitrile endpoint from quantified free arginine, treating sulfite and terminal thioamide substitutions as hypotheses, and avoiding unsupported glutamate-to-ornithine or direct Fischer-Tropsch arginine claims. Reaction-level citations and exact supporting conditions are still missing. P1 provides the strongest supported scaffold, but no pathway establishes a complete operating sequence yielding quantified free arginine. The major limitations are terminal hydrolysis conditions, substrate-specific validation of proposed substitutions, cyanamide guanidination selectivity, and productive ornithine oligomerization. Environmental consistency cannot be strongly established from Surface and Biochemical labels alone: temperature, pH, concentrations, irradiation, catalyst speciation, residence times, reagent delivery and transfer losses need explicit treatment. These are evidentiary and chemical-integration limitations, not penalties for particular feedstocks, shared intermediates, pathway counts or environmental ordering. Overall, this is a credible hypothesis network rather than an approved complete synthesis network; confidence remains below the required 0.90 threshold.
